title: Land Cruiser FJ60
verdict: The FJ60 is the Land Cruiser that learned to carry a family and a cooler without forgetting it was a truck. A carbureted 2F, a four-speed, leaf springs and round headlights make it slow, thirsty and wonderful, provided you can find one whose rear frame rails are still there.

paragraphs: Toyota introduced the 60 Series in 1980, in the middle of the second oil crisis, to compete in a market that was just starting to call itself 'SUV.' It replaced the [[land-cruiser/fj45-fj55|FJ55]] Iron Pig and kept the old recipe underneath: ladder frame, leaf springs and solid axles. What changed was the cabin. Wikipedia lists air conditioning, a rear heater and an upgraded interior. Toyota UK adds that it was the first Land Cruiser with sound insulation and wall-to-wall upholstery, plus a front anti-roll bar and softer springs.

story.heading: A WAGON FOR THE EIGHTIES
paragraphs: The new body was rounder, with front wings integrated into the bodywork for the first time and a wide-set grille. An optional high-roof version arrived in 1981, the same year Land Cruiser sales passed one million. Toyota offered five-, six-, eight-, nine- and ten-seat layouts in different markets, and Flexmotor says the 60 was the first Land Cruiser offered in named trim levels (STD, GX and, later, VX). Silodrome compares the step up in comfort to a Range Rover of the period, which is generous, but not by as much as you'd think.

American FJ60s kept the 4.2-liter 2F straight-six from the [[land-cruiser/fj40|FJ40]], carbureted and rated at 135 hp and 210 lb-ft, with a four-speed manual and a two-speed, part-time transfer case. Other markets moved faster. Wikipedia dates the five-speed to 1982 (Toyota UK says 1983), and says the 4.0-liter carbureted 3F replaced the 2F outside North America in 1984 (as the FJ61), and the 12H-T turbo-diesel appeared in 1985. US buyers got none of that and stuck with the 2F until the [[land-cruiser/fj62|FJ62]] arrived for 1988.

story.heading: LIVING WITH ONE
paragraphs: On the road the FJ60 is slow; Corsetti Cruisers says it tops out around 65 mph. In the dirt it is the same tough truck as the 40, with closed-knuckle Birfield front axles and plenty of clearance. The weak points are age and the smog system. Corsetti lists carburetor rebuilds, tangled vacuum lines, knuckle sludge, steering wobble on lifted trucks, worn engines past 200,000 miles and, above all, rust. Its rust list starts with the windshield corners and ends with the rear wheel wells, which it calls the place every 60 starts to rot.

1981–87 trucks also carry a High Altitude Compensation system that, Corsetti says, advances ignition timing above about 3,930 feet. Many owners have replaced the factory carburetor with a Weber, but Corsetti recommends sticking with the factory carb because the Weber bypasses HAC and brings emissions and jetting headaches. The other common upgrade is a five-speed. In April 1985 Toyota lengthened the H42 four-speed with a spacer where the H55F's fifth gear sits, so on later trucks the five-speed is close to a direct swap.

story.heading: THE COLLECTOR'S 60
paragraphs: The FJ60 gave way to the fuel-injected, automatic [[land-cruiser/fj62|FJ62]] for the 1988 US model year, and Toyota UK says the 60 Series ended Japanese production in December 1989 after 406,700 were built (Wikipedia says 1990), and Venezuela kept assembling them until 1992. For years they were cheap old wagons. Hagerty now calls the round-headlight, manual FJ60 the more collectible of the two, and its wagon-values piece (around 2020) put the median quote for FJ60s and FJ62s at $18,500, with demand apparently overtaking that for Jeep Grand Wagoneers.

That interest has spawned a restomod industry. Shops such as Corsetti Cruisers build FJ60s with modern engines and interiors, while IH8MUD's 60 Series Wagons forum remains the place to learn how to keep a stock one running. The [[land-cruiser/80-series|80 Series]] replaced the whole line in 1990, swapping leaf springs for coils, but the FJ60 has its own following of owners who like its simplicity.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · THE ONE AMERICA DIDN'T GET
callout.title: HJ61: the 60 with the turbo-diesel
paragraphs: Outside North America, the 60 that people talk about is the HJ61. Wikipedia dates the 12H-T direct-injection turbo-diesel to 1985, and Silodrome describes it as a 3,980 cc straight-six with an 18.6:1 compression ratio and 7 psi of boost, making 134 bhp and about 315 lb-ft. Silodrome calls the GX with this engine the most desirable 60.

None were sold new in the US. Under the 25-year import rule they can now be brought in as grey imports. Silodrome says the 12H-T was offered with a five-speed manual or an automatic, and that collectors prefer the manual.

engineering_intro: The FJ60 is a 40 Series drivetrain wearing a family wagon's clothes. It keeps the ladder frame, live axles on leaf springs and closed-knuckle front axle with Birfield joints, and adds a front anti-roll bar, softer springs and power steering. US trucks use the carbureted 2F and an H42 four-speed manual feeding a two-speed, part-time transfer case.

buying_checks.head: Rear frame rails first
buying_checks.body: Corsetti calls it the most important check: drop the spare if you have to and look at the rear frame rails. If the frame is rusted through, walk away. IH8MUD members agree the rear channel near the spare is usually the worst frame spot.

buying_checks.head: The other rust spots
buying_checks.body: Check the windshield gasket corners (peel the rubber back a little), roof drip rails, tailgate hinge areas, inner wheel wells behind the rear seat, front fenders, rockers and rear wheel wells. A missing or uneven mud flap can hide a patched fender, and a magnet finds filler.

buying_checks.head: Floor under the rear seat
buying_checks.body: IH8MUD buyers' threads add the floor pan under the back seat to the list, along with behind the mud flaps.

buying_checks.head: Compression test high-mileage trucks
buying_checks.body: On trucks past 200,000 miles, or that have sat or had several owners, do a compression test. Corsetti's numbers for the 2F: around 160–165 psi is excellent, under 120 means caution, under 100 means don't buy, with no more than 10 percent spread between cylinders.

buying_checks.head: Smog equipment and vacuum lines
buying_checks.body: IH8MUD members call emissions equipment the biggest headache. Check that it's all there, look for cracked or disconnected vacuum hoses, and expect to rebuild the carburetor.

buying_checks.head: Knuckles, steering and power-steering leaks
buying_checks.body: Sludge at the front knuckles means seals are due. Drive it and feel for wobble, especially on a lifted truck. A shiny, wet driver's-side axle and spring usually means the power-steering box or pump is leaking.

buying_checks.head: Budget for rubber
buying_checks.body: Hoses, seals, bushings and diaphragms go hard with age, and most will need replacing. One IH8MUD member put catch-up maintenance at several thousand dollars.

buying_checks.head: Which four-speed?
buying_checks.body: Look for a spacer between the transmission and transfer case. If it's there, it's a post-4/1985 'long' H42, and a five-speed swap is straightforward.

repairs.title: Carburetor rebuild and vacuum check
repairs.symptoms: Stumbling, hesitation, sputtering, rough running or stalling at low rpm. If it only runs with the choke off, suspect the EGR valve.
repairs.fix: Corsetti says the most frequent problem is simply a loose or broken vacuum hose or wiring connection, so check fuel and ignition basics, then every vacuum line, before blaming the carb. Rebuild the factory carburetor and check the EGR valve while you're there. Above 3,930 feet, check the High Altitude Compensation system, which a Weber carb bypasses. Trucks over 200,000 miles will likely need a full set of vacuum hoses.
repairs.tools: Carb rebuild kit · vacuum hose · vacuum diagram · vacuum gauge · carb cleaner

repairs.title: Compression test before you buy or rebuild
repairs.symptoms: Low power, blow-by or an unknown engine history on a truck past 200,000 miles.
repairs.fix: With the engine warm, pull all six plugs, disable the ignition, hold the throttle open and crank each cylinder for the same number of strokes. Corsetti's guide for a healthy 2F is 160–165 psi, with caution under 120 and walk away under 100. Readings should be within 10 percent of each other. Significant wear usually means valves, seats and rings, so a full rebuild.
repairs.tools: Compression gauge · spark-plug socket · remote starter switch

parts.name: Spark plug wire set, premium reproduction, FJ40/45/60 1980–87

repairs.title: Front knuckle rebuild
repairs.symptoms: Grease sludge leaking from the steering knuckles where axle grease has got past the seals.
repairs.fix: Pull the hub, spindle and Birfield, remove the knuckle caps and bearings, replace the inner axle seal, knuckle bearings and wiper seals, then repack and reassemble. Top shims set knuckle-bearing preload. On 1981 trucks, check whether the factory steering recall parts were fitted.
repairs.tools: Spring scale · seal driver · Cruiser Corps kit 595-102 or 514-109 · knuckle shim and gasket kit 595-101 · moly grease

repairs.title: Cure the death wobble
repairs.symptoms: Violent front-end shake after a bump, especially on lifted trucks; or a shake you feel in the truck but not the steering wheel.
repairs.fix: Inspect tie-rod ends, the drag link, knuckle preload and the steering box mounts first. Corsetti fits an Old Man Emu steering damper to every FJ60, lifted or not. Expect the factory stabilizer to be hard to remove without an air tool. If the wheel is calm but the truck still shakes, the driveshaft probably needs balancing, which is common past 200,000 miles.
repairs.tools: Impact wrench · Old Man Emu steering damper (OMESD24 in OME's 60 Series kits)

repairs.title: H55F five-speed swap
repairs.time: ≈ A weekend; the pilot bearing took Off-Road.com's author a full day
repairs.cost: Parts plus labor; flywheel resurfacing about $30
repairs.symptoms: About 3,250 rpm at 75 mph in fourth gear.
repairs.fix: On post-4/1985 trucks the H55F is direct-fit. Drain and remove the driveshafts, starter, clutch slave and transfer-case shift lever, support the engine and drop the four-speed. Replace the clutch, pilot bearing and rear main seal, resurface the flywheel, then fit the H55F with its fifth-gear oiler, plug the crossbar hole in the transfer case and use new gaskets and staked nuts. Pre-4/1985 trucks also need shift-linkage and driveshaft changes. The 0.84 fifth drops highway rpm to about 2,750 at 75 mph.
repairs.tools: Transmission jack · 32 mm and 36 mm sockets · clutch alignment tool · clutch kit · gaskets · fifth-gear oiler

repairs.title: Replace the front heater core
repairs.symptoms: Coolant smell in the cabin, a damp passenger carpet, poor heat or unexplained coolant loss.
repairs.fix: Drain the coolant, disconnect the heater hoses at the firewall, remove the dash panels and heater box, and swap the core. Refill and bleed. Cruiser Corps warns that a leaking core can corrode the floorboards under wet carpet, so dry and check the floor while it's apart.
repairs.tools: Basic hand tools · coolant · Cruiser Corps 520-127 front heater core (8/1980–8/1987)

repairs.title: Two-inch lift with fresh springs
repairs.cost: Old Man Emu kits about $2,400 (Cruiser Corps)
repairs.symptoms: Sagging leaf springs, worn shocks or a nose-down stance.
repairs.fix: Old Man Emu sells 2-inch kits for FJ60s in light, medium and heavy load ratings, split at April 1985. They include springs, Nitrocharger shocks, greaseable anti-inversion shackles and pins, bushings, U-bolts and a steering damper. Change one axle at a time with the frame supported, and grease the new shackles and pins.
repairs.tools: Jacks and stands · breaker bar · ARB/OME kit (pre- or post-4/1985) · grease gun

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: 33x9.50 fits on stock suspension; one IH8MUD member runs them on a stock FJ62 with 240,000 miles. 33x10.50 might fit, but 33x12.50s won't without a lift: one '87 FJ60 on a 2.5-inch BDS lift still rubbed its inner wheel wells at full stuff. Corsetti runs 31x10.50R15s on stock springs and says not to go wider than 10.5 in or taller than 33 in on a factory rim; Cruiser Corps also advises against tires wider than 10.5 in on the 15x5.5 OEM steel wheel.

The FJ60 (US 1981–87) has round headlights, the carbureted 4.2 L 2F and a four-speed manual. The [[land-cruiser/fj62|FJ62]] (1988–90) has fuel injection, an automatic, square headlights and a plusher cabin. Hagerty calls the FJ60 the more collectible. The FJ62 is easier to live with in traffic.

faq.q: Did US FJ60s get a five-speed?
faq.a: No. US trucks used the H41F/H42F four-speed. The H55F five-speed went into other markets from 1982–83, and swapping one in is close to direct on post-April-1985 US trucks.

faq.q: What's the High Altitude Compensation system?
faq.a: It's emissions equipment on 1981–87 trucks that Corsetti says advances ignition timing above about 3,930 feet. A Weber carburetor bypasses it and costs performance, so Corsetti recommends keeping the factory carb.

faq.q: What fuel economy should I expect?
faq.a: Corsetti lists 11 mpg city and 18 highway with a 23.8-gallon tank. In practice, bigger tires and a roof rack make it worse.

faq.q: How do I tell if the engine is tired?
faq.a: Do a compression test. Corsetti's benchmarks for a 2F are about 160–165 psi when excellent, caution under 120 and walk away under 100, with no more than 10 percent spread. The 2F reportedly reaches 300,000 miles with care.

The classic setup is an Old Man Emu 2-inch kit with greaseable shackles and a steering damper. Kits are split by build date (before or after April 1985) and load rating. Corsetti fits an OME steering damper even on unlifted trucks.

faq.q: Can I import a diesel HJ61?
faq.a: None were sold new in the US, but the 25-year rule now covers every 60 Series. Silodrome calls the 12H-T-powered GX the most desirable 60. Check EPA and state registration rules before buying.

Hagerty's wagon-values piece (around 2020) put the median quote for FJ60s and FJ62s at $18,500, called the FJ60 the pick for collectibility and said demand appeared to be overtaking Jeep Grand Wagoneers. Rust-free restored and restomod trucks sell for much more.

baseline_service.intro: An FJ60 is now 40-plus years old and most have passed 200,000 miles, so treat every fluid and grease point as unknown. Fluid types and capacities below are from Toyota publications as compiled on IH8MUD for the 60 and 70 series (US FJ60: 2F engine and H41F/H42F four-speed; the H55F five-speed was never fitted to US trucks at the factory).
